This 1930's thor style wringer washer was amongst the junk when I visited my home before buying it a few years back, I asked to have it & it's been in storage ever since.

I finally decided it was time for a rebuild to start using it. I did 2 washes in it for kick & honestly, it's simplicity, effectiveness & strength is actually putting modern washers to shame imo.

Unfortunately G.E. Canada didn't have any info on hand about this model, I'll have to check with the science & tech museum.

The wringer & its gearbox. It didn't look too bad, it came apart pretty easily... the gearbox contents were so messy I stopped taking pics so I wouldn't wreck my phone. Here's the bottom gear box once opened., it's only 80 to 90yo after all.

I sent everything but the enameled tub to the paint shop we use at work for a good sandblast, a zinc rich primer & finally a nice thick coat of ral 5015 powder coat. The chromed part from the wringer I had painted as well, there aren't too many chrome shops around here and I didn't want to spend too much either.

Then I turned my attention to the gears, all cast iron. They obviously needed a good cleaning so I scuffed them with one of those zim-zim air tools, took me aboot an hour to get them all cleaned up. I noticed that the gear used to select the direction in which the wringer turns had previously been rebuilt

The main gear for the washer action was also hurting a bit as well as the other 2 wringer drive gears. I brazed them with bronse & filed them down.

Here they are all layed out..

...and the rest of the parts back from the paint shop:

https://images2.imgbox.com/d4/e5/MnCpLuIr_o.jpg

https://images2.imgbox.com/e2/94/jyZvLeJh_o.jpg

https://images2.imgbox.com/f8/60/ISzvEwTh_o.jpg

Now came the fun part, putting everything back together. I started with the main gearbox, had to get the flanges cleaned up.

https://images2.imgbox.com/10/05/c9FUu7fN_o.jpg

https://images2.imgbox.com/8c/7b/B5pYCalV_o.jpg

The old hydraulic seal & its housing, which seals the shaft coming out of the gear box, was dead & unusable so I had a new one machined and pressed it into place. Then it was time to cut a new gasket and put the gears back into place.

The wringer gearbox has a locking pin that holds it in different positions on the shaft. Once that was back in place I layed out the gears, shoved everything back in, packed it with grease & closed it up.

Next I got the main washer clutch assembly together and reassembled.. It's actually the pivot point for the washer gear which sits on an offset sliding cam and that makes the shaft it powers go swoosh swoosh when you engage the clutch.

Filled the main gearbox with oil and then I closed it up.

The last part I had to reassemble was the wringer. I didn't bother with the rollers yet as I'm still looking at options, here they are with their wood block bushings & the polished agitator.

I got the roll pressure spring & safety bars back together, then the whatever these are called onto the frame and reassembled the wringer.

The motor I took apart to clean up, changed the brushes & contacts along with a new cord & GFI plug.

It was finally time to put it all back together, the tub's enamel was still in pristine condition so I won't get it redone just yet.

Here it is, a fully functioning 1930's Thor style wringer washer manufactured by General Electric Canada in Ontario.

Total cost:

Parts (gaskets & seals, machining, cleaning products, oil & grease): 250$

The paint job I got for free because I'm treated that well by my subcontractors at work :)

Time spent, roughly 12 hours.
